title: How Inmates Eat, Shower & Sleep in America's Only Federal Supermax
asof: Figures from the 2018 DC CIC inspection (visit 2017) · sources in description

shots.s: There's a prison in Colorado built so you never see another prisoner.
Your room is seven feet by twelve.
The bed is concrete.
The desk is concrete.
Your window is four inches wide.
And all it shows you is the sky.
You'll spend at least twenty-two hours a day in here.
So how do you eat,
shower,
and sleep,
in America's only federal supermax?
This is ADX Florence.
It opened in 1994, in the high desert south of Colorado Springs.
It's the only federal prison of its kind.
Its official name is Administrative Maximum.
Reporters call the people inside the worst of the worst.
It was built for four hundred and ninety men.
In 2017, it held four hundred and twenty-seven.
Most aren't here for the crime they committed.
They're here for how they behaved in other prisons.
You arrive in chains.
Every trip out of a cell takes an escort of guards.
Cells sit in a line down one side of the hallway.
It's built that way so no prisoner can see another.
Here's everything you own now.
A bed, poured from concrete.
A concrete desk.
A concrete stool.
None of it moves.
A steel sink and toilet, in one piece.
The bed has handles built into it.
They're for strapping a prisoner down.
Then there's the door.
Actually, two doors.
A barred door on the inside.
A solid steel door on the outside.
The window is about forty-two inches tall.
And four inches wide.
It's angled so you can only see the sky.
No ground.
No trees.
No mountains.
There's no dining hall.
Meals are carried from the kitchen to your door.
The door has a slot.
Your tray comes through it.
You eat alone, at your concrete desk.
Three meals a day, every day.
The budget?
About three dollars and fifty cents a day per prisoner.
The cooks are prisoners too, from the camp next door.
In a survey, about a third complained about the food.
One man said the portions are terrible.
Another said they never change the menu.
For many men, the trays are the main time they see anyone.
One put it this way:
we only see staff when they feed us,
pick up the trays,
and at recreation.
In most units, the shower is inside your cell.
That way, you never have to leave to wash.
It shuts off on its own.
The water can't run forever,
so nobody floods the range.
In the step-down units, it's different.
There, the showers sit in a shared room.
At night, you sleep on that concrete slab.
There's a thin mattress on top.
Nobody shares the cell.
You might get a radio or a small TV.
It's your main window to the world.
Books come from the library, one request at a time.
And then it's six AM again.
Out-of-cell time is about two hours each weekday.
That's ten hours a week.
Three to five officers escort you there.
While you're out, they search your cell.
Some days you go indoors, to an almost empty room.
Other days you go outside.
Outside means a cage, in a deep concrete pit.
There's a mesh roof over your head.
You can shout to a few other men in their cages.
In the Control Unit, even that's gone.
There, men stay inside twenty-three to twenty-four hours a day.
In general population, you get up to three phone calls a month.
Fifteen minutes each.
Each long-distance call costs three dollars and forty-five cents.
There's no email.
Visits are never contact visits.
You sit behind glass and talk on a phone.
Thirty-four days a year, no visits are allowed at all.
And Colorado is far from most families.
One man hadn't seen his family since 2003.
Another man can't shop at the commissary until the year twenty-one hundred.
A government report quoted a psychologist who worked there.
On the most isolated range, they said, you have no contact.
You don't speak to anybody.
They called it a form of torture on some level.
In 2012, prisoners with mental illness sued the prison system.
The case was settled in 2016.
A former warden once called ADX a clean version of hell.
Many men here can work their way out.
First, a full year with no trouble.
Then a step-down unit, with a shared room and other people.
After about six months, a transfer next door.
There, you get a cellmate for the first time in years.
Then another prison.
Staff say it's designed as a two-year process.
For the men who never finish it,
the sky through that four-inch window is the view for years.
Could you last a week in that room?
